title: Light a burned-down jar candle with a utility lighter: latch held in while pulling the trigger, nozzle deep in the jar
instruction: Light the candle in the glass jar with the utility lighter, then put the lighter down on the table.
context: Lighting a jar candle with a long utility lighter is an everyday home job, and a burned-down jar is why such lighters exist: its wick sits deep below the rim, out of reach of a match. Every utility lighter sold in the US must be child-resistant: the trigger is blocked until a separate latch is pressed. BIC's answer on its Multi-Purpose Lighter's retail page: "hold the utility lighter with your thumb resting on the latch and your index finger on the trigger" ... "depress the latch with the tip of your thumb and hold in" ... "pull the trigger with your index finger". The hand skill differs from lighting a dinner candle with a match: one grip must press a 3 mm latch fully in and keep it in while pulling a 10 mm trigger (12 N) and not before, so a careless pinch on the trigger alone does nothing; and the 10 mm nozzle must go 3 cm down into an 85 mm jar, to a wick 3.7 cm below the rim, without knocking the glass, then come out and be put down. One arm is enough.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table. Both arms at the ready pose, grippers open. Glass jar candle, loose (650 g): clear glass jar 8.5 cm across and 10 cm tall (4 mm wall, 8 mm base) centred at (24, 0), dark red wax up to 5.5 cm, a cotton wick standing 8 mm out of the middle of the wax (tip 6.3 cm up, 3.7 cm below the rim). Utility lighter, loose (60 g), the size of a BIC Multi-Purpose Classic: red handle 10.5 x 3 x 2.4 cm, metal wand 15 cm long and 1 cm across from the handle's front end (25.5 cm overall), lying on its side with its handle centred at (15, -17), wand pointing to +y (nozzle tip at about (15.7, 3.3)), latch side facing forward. Latch: black button 14 x 12 mm on top of the handle, 4.2 cm behind its front end, 3 mm proud, pressed in 3 mm (4.5 N fully in). Trigger: black, 24 x 10 mm, 12 mm out of the underside, 1 cm behind the front end, pulled 10 mm in (12 N fully in); it stops after 2 mm unless the latch is in 2.5 mm or more. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Every 50 ms: latch and trigger travel, lighter and jar poses, finger points. Gas flows while the latch is in 2.5 mm or more and the trigger 8 mm or more; a 25 mm flame then stands on the nozzle tip along the wand. The wick lights once its tip has been within 6 mm of that flame for 1.0 s in all. 0.5 candle lit; 0.75 also the lighter put down: on the table (lowest point under 2 cm up, still), gas off, every finger point 2 cm or more from it; 1.0 (held 1 s) also the jar upright (under 10 deg) and within 2 cm of its start. 0 for the run if the jar ever tilts 30 deg or more. Real trial: a filled lighter, the candle seen burning 2 s after the lighter's flame is gone (or an emptied lighter, the same rule judged from side video); jar checked against marks with a tape measure.
reset_notes: Real trials: snuff the candle with a lid or snuffer (never blow wax), let the jar cool, trim the wick to 8 mm, put the jar on its marks; lay the lighter on its side on its marks. Work on a non-flammable tray with an extinguisher at hand; keep the flame inside the jar. Simulation: each trial starts afresh.
fidelity: Rigid bodies (PhysX), 20 Hz. No gas or fire: the flame and the wick catching are a rule on the latch, the trigger and where the nozzle points (25 mm flame, wick within 6 mm for 1 s), drawn as visual flames. The latch, trigger, their springs and the trigger's 2 mm block are physical (the block is a joint limit set while the latch is out). Spring forces are estimates. Glass, wax and the wick are rigid; the jar is a 20-sided shell.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (it brought the right gripper to the lighter and hovered beside its handle for the rest of the run, never picking it up); demo: 1.0
